newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Rivals fight for Kabul despite U.N. truce call.
newsitem.headline: Rivals fight for Kabul despite U.N. truce call.

text.p: The Afghan government sent fresh troops to frontlines around Kabul to hold off the rebel Taleban militia as the two sides fought on Thursday, ignoring a U.N. Security Council call for an immediate ceasefire.
The government forces held off overnight Taleban attacks from southeast and southwest of the capital and deployed fresh troops on all frontlines, Defence Ministry sources said.
The Taleban attacks came from Butkhak, about 20 km (12 miles) southeast of Kabul, and Koh-i-Koruk, about 20 km to the southwest, they said.
More than 150 rebel fighters were killed in a four-hour battle for a customs house in eastern Kabul starting at midnight, the sources said.

They said the customs house was now no-man's land, but government forces held the nearby Pul-i-Charkhi jail, which Taleban sources in neighbouring Pakistan said had been captured by the militia. There were several government air raids in Pul-i-Charkhi village on Wednesday evening.

A Taleban source in the northwest Pakistani town of Peshawar earlier said the militia forces had penetrated eastern Kabul overnight and were only about five km (three miles) from the presidential palace.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) also quoted other Taleban sources as saying the militia had broken through government lines in the south and southwest of Kabul.
There was no independent confirmation of these reports.
Hospital sources in Kabul said at least three civilians were killed and 21 wounded by overnight Taleban rocketing on Kabul.

The Defence Ministry sources denied a Taleban claim that the militia forces had advanced up the Tagab valley close to the main government airbase of Bagram, north of Kabul, and said the area was firmly in government control.
Government fighters packed on tanks and armoured personnel carriers headed towards the frontlines, witnesses said.

Kabul city was calm, and shops and markets were open with no visible sign of panic. But hundreds of people were leaving the city on the road north towards Mazar-i-Sharif in trucks and buses packed with belongings on roofs.
"Nothing has changed in Kabul, but people are afraid of the future," an Afghan aid worker said.

At least 20 foreign aid workers were evacuated from Bagram on two flights arranged by the International Committee of the Red Cross on Thursday as Afghan passengers were getting ready to board a flight of the state airline Ariana to the Indian capital of New Delhi.
Five Ariana planes were parked at Bagram airport along with several MI-8 helicopter gunships and MiG fighters.

"They (government fighters) set up a machine-gun in my street so I thought I had better leave," said Jeff Arnold, programme officer of the German Agro-Action relief agency. "I hope this will all be over quickly so we can come back."
"The Taleban are coming, one hundred percent," an Afghan aid worker said.
An APC guarded the entrance to Bagram airport and a government commander sped towards Kabul with three vehicles full of troops.
AIP said fighting raged in the eastern suburbs of Kabul on Thursday morning after a comparative lull overnight, with the Taleban holding positions it had captured on Wednesday.
A Taleban source in Peshawar denied a Kabul government report on Wednesday night that its forces had repulsed the militia from the east of the capital.

The source, speaking anonymously, said Taleban forces entered the city from Pul-i-Charkhi village, which they said they had captured on Wednesday in a swift advance after seizing the strategic eastern town of Sarobi.
Official Kabul Radio said on Wednesday night the Taleban had cut off electricity to Kabul only 10 days after it was restored to part of the city from an eastern power house after two years.
The 15-nation U.N. Security Council made an appeal for a ceasefire and peace talks after a meeting in New York.

"The members of the council call upon the parties to stop fighting immediately, to agree to a ceasefire and to enter into serious negotiations to find a political solution to this conflict," the current council president, Alfredo Lopes Cabral of Guinea-Bissau, told reporters.
The council, which has made similar appeals before without success, was particularly concerned by the humanitarian crisis and the risk of civilian casualties in the fighting for Kabul.
The Afghan government asked the Security Council to meet on the crisis and accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban. Pakistan has denied any involvement in the conflict.
